## My data
The Fairness section uses an Adult income dataset with 5,000 observations. The plots examine income, sex, race, capital gains, and weekly working hours.

```{r}
#| label: data
#| echo: true
```

### A1 · Label it

```{r}
#| label: fig-a1
#| ref.label: a1
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Share of each group with the outcome, labeled for a reader."
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal stacked bar chart comparing income groups by sex."
```

```{r}
#| label: a1-check
#| include: false
```

The legend title was the label I changed most because the original TRUE and FALSE values were not very descriptive. I changed it to "Income above $50K" to make the outcome clearer. I also added a descriptive title and percentage axis labels. A reader can understand the comparison without needing additional explanations.

### A2 · Choose a scale

```{r}
#| label: fig-a2
#| ref.label: a2
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "My scale choice."
#| fig-alt: "Histogram showing positive capital gains on a logarithmic scale."
```

```{r}
#| label: a2-check
#| include: false
```

I used a logarithmic scale because capital gains are highly right-skewed. It makes smaller positive values easier to examine alongside larger values. I excluded 4,563 zero or negative values because they cannot be displayed on a logarithmic scale.

### A3 · Facet it: fixed or free

```{r}
#| label: fig-a3
#| ref.label: a3
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "The same rates in panels: fixed and free y-axes."
#| fig-subcap: ["Fixed", "Free"]
#| fig-alt: "Faceted column charts comparing income percentages by sex and race, with fixed and free scales."
#| layout: [[1, 1]]
```

```{r}
#| label: a3-chosen
#| include: false
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-a3
#| tbl-cap: "Each group's n and rate, by panel."
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(a3_rates, digits = 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: a3-check
#| include: false
```

I chose fixed scales because using the same percentage range makes comparisons between race groups easier. Males had a higher percentage earning above $50,000 in every race group. Some groups had small sample sizes, such as Other (42 people) and American Indian-Eskimo (47 people).

### A4 · Compared to what?

```{r}
#| label: fig-a4
#| ref.label: a4
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Two groups: individual values and resampled means, same axes."
#| fig-alt: "Faceted jitter plots comparing individual and resampled weekly working hours by sex."
```

```{r}
#| label: a4-check
#| include: false
```

The individual values overlap considerably, meaning both groups have a wide range of working hours. However, the resampled group means are clearly separated, with males having a higher average weekly working time around 40 hours. This shows that individual differences can overlap even when group averages are different.

## Part B · Sports

### B1 · Label it

```{r}
#| label: fig-b1
#| ref.label: b1
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "My Sports plot, labeled for a reader."
#| fig-alt: "Horizontal stacked bar chart comparing match duration groups by court surface."
```

```{r}
#| label: b1-check
#| include: false
```

I changed the x-axis label the most because the plot shows percentages rather than raw counts. I labeled it "Share of matches (%)" to make that clear. The title, subtitle, and legend also explain what is being compared, so a reader can understand the plot without additional explanation.

### B2 · Choose a scale

```{r}
#| label: fig-b2
#| ref.label: b2
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "My scale choice."
#| fig-alt: "Histogram showing winner rankings on a logarithmic scale."
```

```{r}
#| label: b2-check
#| include: false
```

I used a logarithmic scale because winner rankings are right-skewed. It makes the distribution easier to examine by showing smaller and larger rankings together. Five observations with missing rankings were removed, while no zero or negative values needed to be excluded.

### B3 · Facet it: fixed or free

```{r}
#| label: fig-b3
#| ref.label: b3
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "The same plot in panels: fixed and free y-axes."
#| fig-subcap: ["Fixed", "Free"]
#| fig-alt: "Faceted column charts comparing long-match percentages by court surface and year, with fixed and free scales."
#| layout: [[1, 1]]
```

```{r}
#| label: b3-check
#| include: false
```

I chose fixed scales because they allow readers to compare match percentages across years using the same y-axis range. This makes differences easier to compare, but smaller changes may be harder to notice. The smallest panels were 2020 and 2022, with 381 matches each. Hard courts had the highest percentage of long matches in 2018, 2019, and 2022, while Clay had the highest in 2020 and 2021. These are differences in the data, not evidence of causes.

### B4 · Compared to what?

```{r}
#| label: fig-b4
#| ref.label: b4
#| echo: true
#| fig-cap: "Two groups: individual values and resampled means, same axes."
#| fig-alt: "Faceted jitter plots comparing individual and resampled match durations on Hard and Clay courts."
```

```{r}
#| label: b4-check
#| include: false
```

The individual values overlap considerably, meaning Clay and Hard court matches can have similar durations, with plenty of variation within each surface. The resampled means are also very close, showing that the average match durations for the two surfaces are nearly the same, even though individual match lengths vary widely.

```{r}

```

```{r}
#| label: b5-check
#| include: false
```

I colored by the surface column to distinguish Clay, Grass, and Hard courts. I used the Viridis color scale because it provides distinguishable colors. My plot passed the color check without needing to change the categories. In all three simulated views, the categories remain distinguishable.

## One thing I tried in my slides, and why
I used a finding-based headline instead of a general topic title: “Males had a higher percentage of adults earning above $50,000 in every race group.” This tells the audience the main finding before they look at the chart and makes the comparison easier to follow.
